children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK
For millions of Americans who rely on SNAP, buying groceries involves a routine swipe of a government-issued benefits card. That swipe has become an opening for organized crime.

Romanian crime groups are using skimming devices to steal SNAP recipients' account numbers and PINs, part of a sprawling racket that authorities say has swindled hundreds of millions of dollars in public benefits across the U.S. Their advantage is surprisingly simple: Many of the cards used to distribute SNAP benefits still rely on magnetic-stripe technology invented in the 1960s.

Authorities say cash in the form of crypto is sent back to Romania, where money flows into real estate, gambling and crime bosses. But the losses are felt in the U.S. by people who can least afford them. Scott Calvert and Dan Frosch trace how Romanian gangs built a global racket around a weakness in America's benefits system and the efforts to stop them.

Treasury yields have surged sharply this year, but Federal Reserve models offer conflicting explanations for the reasons, writes James Mackintosh.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Polymarket's aggressive push to scale left its platform wide open to fraudsters.

Earlier this year, thieves flooded its U.S. betting platform with stolen debit cards, trying to make off with at least $10 million. At one point, more than 80% of deposits handled by a payment processor were rejected as fraudulent, far above industry standards of roughly 1%. When employees raised concerns, CEO Shayne Coplan told them to keep growing and pay a fine if regulators found out, according to people familiar with the events. Our reporters interviewed current and former employees and reviewed text messages to investigate the problems behind Polymarket's rapid expansion ahead of a potential IPO.
5. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK

Senior Video Journalist Jaden Urbi: I started reporting this story because I wanted to know why so many men are obsessed with Iron Heart jeans. The answer revealed a lot more than just "Japanese craftsmanship."

The Japanese denim industry is the product of Hollywood's cultural exports, a U.S. military occupation, Japan's quest to rebuild its economy, American offshoring, clunky old internet forums and some very interesting characters.

I spent a day in Zurich with a 67-year-old man who goes by "Swiss Jeans Freak." He has over 14,000 denim items, some of which he saved from dumpsters, others were donated, and some are his own unwashed pairs of raw denim jeans. That's what he calls "extreme denimhead" behavior: wearing jeans for 1,000+ days to get the coolest fades. Yes, there was an odor.

But what really struck me was that behind the obsession is a genuine community of people who actually know each other. The Iron Heart Forum is one of the last raw denim forums that is still thriving. It's not driven by an algorithm, and frankly, it's a nightmare to navigate, but that's part of its charm. Its more than 17,000 members have daily conversations about denim, but also about what they're cooking, watching and listening to.

And every so often, members of the so-called Iron Heart Army step out from behind the screen, get on a plane and fly across the world to spend a few days hanging out with the people they chat with online every day. That feels meaningful.

6. SEE THE STORY
Step inside the massive data centers powering America's AI boom.

Behind nondescript exteriors in Virginia's "Data Center Alley," some employees log up to 30,000 steps a day while others ride scooters down echoey hallways and sniff for overheating equipment. We take you inside the daily lives of the workers keeping AI online, from engineers checking rooftops for bird damage to technicians hunkering down on cots during extreme weather to keep servers running 24/7.

Thursday: Trump hosts Xi at the White House for bilateral summit talks and a formal state dinner. Costco reports earnings.
8. THE NUMBER

That was the median sale price in June for a single-family home in the U.S. with two bedrooms or fewer, according to Zillow. By comparison, the median price of an existing home in the U.S., across home sizes, was around $430,000. Smaller homes can offer buyers a more affordable way into today's difficult housing market, but there's a catch: Homes with two bedrooms or fewer made up just 14% of listings. Still, buyers who move a little farther from the city, buy a smaller home or settle for more modest finishes are finding that it is still possible to buy.
9. AND FINALLY...
Even star chefs sometimes just want instant ramen.

Kwame Onwuachi is behind Tatiana, one of New York's toughest reservations, but at home he reaches for the Top Ramen he grew up eating. His "triple-deluxe" version adds real shrimp, crab and seafood broth, turning the instant noodles into something special without making them much harder to cook. He shares his recipe with us, along with the secret to his go-to spice blend.
